title: Replacing Roy Johnson; reading chord symbols
summary: With ten days to learn the book, Monk relied on chord symbols and his ear, practicing electric off stage.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

Roy Johnson, who was working his two weeks out.
That gave me a chance, when we speak about me being qualified
to go in and sight read the music, from the standpoint of how
did I get into it, well, with the two-week period...It wasn't,
I guess it was about a ten day period...I had a chance, the
opportunity to become acquainted with the music. Because by
the time I arrived in San Francisco and we made our way up the
Coast, well, I'm looking, about ten days to learn the music.
So, by being accustomed to...That was, my music was...The
expression was 'playing off of what I heard.' It wasn't...
You weren't much of a reader.

No, But I will have to admit, I had spent some time with musicians that...I'm reading chord symbols. I knew chord symbols well enough to know chord symbols, you know. And fortunately enough, the majority of the music that Hamp had in his book, there were chord symbols over all the four-bar changes. Within every four bars, wherever the changes are, maybe every two bars, whatever. But there were symbols written.
And you could handle that easier than you could handle the actual written-out line.

Right. I couldn't handle the lines and spaces, so it was just symbols. But Hamp's music, there was really nothing tricky about his music. I mean, if you just knew where the breaks were at. You know, enough to hear, and being familiar enough with Hamp's music, a ballad or something like that, with a thing that's an extra edge for a bass player that's not, that don't have the qualifications of reading lines and spaces...If he can read chord signatures, he'll see a chord symbol, and the chord symbol might be a Bb7. Well, you don't have to really be an Einstein to figure out a good note to play out of a Bb7, of that chord. You know, you don't have to play the precise note that some arranger has written out for you. It might have sound...chords that sound better...but for that I had a pretty good ear.

I've often seen cases where a bass player, since we're talking about the instrument, would have a better concept of notes to use in a chord than the guy who might be writing it, because he's just writing basic chord symbols down, you know. We may have a better choice of note to play against the chord.

Anyhow, with that little knowledge I had about chord symbols, plus I could hear what was going on...I remember there were times when the bass player, Roy Johnson, the bass player before me, was playing with the band and I could...I'd have the instrument out, playing along with it, off stage.
Yeah, because I had to get used to this fellow. I had to get accustomed to it...

...playing horizontal rather than up, you know, the whole strength of it, the whole everything was different. And it felt strange and foreign in my hands. So I spent my days, in the day, practicing. Not really happy with what I was doing, but I had to readjust and part of that practice time was spent readjusting. It wasn't just simply practicing.
Readjusting to the choice you had made.
